source: That branch of the lake of Como which extends southwards between two unbroken chains of mountains, and is all bays and gulfs as the mountains advance and recede, narrows down at one point into the form of a river, between a promontory on one side and a wide shore on the other; and the bridge which here links the two banks seems to emphasize this transformation, and to mark the point at which the lake ends and the Adda begins, only to become a lake once more where the banks draw farther apart again, letting the water broaden out and expand into new gulfs and bays. The country bordering the lake, formed by the deposits of three great torrents, is backed by two neighbouring mountains, one called San Martino, and the other, in the Lombard dialect, the Resegone, from its saw-like row of peaks; so that on first seeing it — so long as it is in profile — looking northwards, for instance, from the ramparts of Milan — one can pick it out at once, on the name alone, from the vast and lengthy range of other mountains of obscurer name and more ordinary form. For a considerable stretch the country rises slowly and continuously; then it breaks up into little hills and valleys and into steep and level tracts, following the structure of the two mountains and the erosion of the water. The shore itself, intersected by the beds of torrents, is almost entirely gravel and pebbles; the rest is fields and vineyards, and scattered towns, villages and farms, with here and there a wood extending right on up the mountain-side. Lecco, which is the largest of these towns and gives its name to the district, lies on the lakeside not far from the bridge, and is even apt to find itself partly in the lake when this is high; it is a big town nowadays, well on the way to becoming a city. At the time of the events which we are about to describe, this township which was already of some importance, was also fortified, and so had the honour of housing a commandant and the advantage of a permanent garrison of Spanish soldiers, who taught modesty to the wives and daughters of the town, tickled up the shoulders of an occasional husband and father, and, towards the end of summer, never failed to scatter themselves among the vineyards, to thin out the grapes and lighten the labours of the vintage for the peasants. Paths and tracks used to run — and still do — from one to another of these villages, from the mountain heights to the lakeside, and from one precipice to the other. Sometimes they run steep, sometimes level, and often drop suddenly and bury themselves between two walls, from which, when one looks up, only a patch of sky and some mountain peak can be discerned. Sometimes they come out on open terraces; thence the eye ranges over prospects of varying extent, always full of interest and always changing, as each point of vantage takes in different aspects of the vast landscape, and as one part or the other is foreshortened, or stands out, or disappears. One can see a piece here, another there, and then again a long stretch of that great varied mirror of the water; on this side the lake is shut in at one end, or rather lost among the ins and outs and groupings of the mountains, then spreads out again between more mountains, unfolding one by one, and reflected upside down in the water with the villages on the shores; on the other side is more river, then lake, then river again, losing itself in a shining coil among the mountains, which follow it, getting smaller and smaller until they too are almost lost in the horizon. The very spot from which so many different views can be seen itself appears in views from every side. The mountain on whose foothills you are walking unfolds its cliffs and pinnacles above and around you, each standing out on its own and changing at every step, turning what had just seemed a single ridge into a whole series of ridges, and showing on a height something that a moment before had seemed down on the shore; the quiet and cosy character of these foothills pleasantly tempers the wildness around, and is a foil for the grandeur of the rest of the landscape.

rows.text:
The sea between two continents narrows here into a corridor of traffic that no chart confesses, and where the African shelf climbs toward the sunken ridge the water pales from ink to a bruised turquoise, and the swell loses its ocean length and begins to chop; and out of that paleness a low island lifts itself, bare as a knuckle, a slab of limestone tilted so that its back is turned to Europe and its face, worn to rubble by the sirocco, leans south toward the Libyan coast, which is nearer than Sicily, so that a boat setting out at dusk from Zuwarah need only hold its heading until morning to find the shoals, and the lamps come up out of the dark.

The island is eight miles of karst, which holds no river and almost no soil, which feeds its dry-stone terraces on dew and the memory of rain, which has taught its few pines to crouch sideways under the wind rather than grow upright; it is rimmed everywhere with cliffs, except where the limestone splits at Cala Croce and the swimmers go down, except where the Bay of Rabbits opens its white arc to the turtles, except where the harbour cuts its single deep notch into the southern flank.

Into that notch the whole business of the frontier has been folded, and it sits there in the plain light of the quay like any other piece of municipal plumbing, while the ferry from Porto Empedocle unloads its crates of mineral water.

Along the mole there run the grey hulls of the patrol service, whose numbers are stencilled in white on their bows; they lie three abreast in the shallow basin, where the fuel skin turns the water to a slow rainbow.

Above them a mast of sensors stands on the ridge at Albero Sole, which turns all night and takes the curvature of the sea into its arithmetic, measuring returns too small to be hulls until the operator leans forward and enlarges them; and below it the prefabricated sheds of the reception centre sit in a fold of the Imbriacola valley, screened by a fence that is designed not to be visible from the road.

The apparatus has its own geology here, which can be read in strata like the rock, which is older in some courses than in others: the stone jetty of the Bourbon port lies at the bottom, and above it the concrete of the air base, and above that the fibre-optic trunk, the thermal cameras, the EU-funded floodlights that burn the headland white at two in the morning, so that the island keeps no true darkness any longer, and the shearwaters cry over the glare.

The place is thus two geographies at once, each pretending not to notice the other, and the tourists photograph the turquoise from the clifftop while the radio rooms log the night's contacts.

The cemetery of the unnamed lies behind a wall to seaward, numbered, not named; the markers are cheap and the weeds take them quickly, and the fishermen pass them going up to the road, because the shortest way home runs through it.

Everything on the island is a matter of distance and of paperwork: the crossing is a hundred and twenty sea miles, and the register of arrivals is kept in a ledger where the hour is entered, and the nationality declared, and the number given.

What governs the island is not the mayor and not the sea but the hinge between them: the boats come when the wind drops below force four, and the centre fills past its capacity, which was set at four hundred and is routinely eight times that, and then the transfers begin. It is a rhythm that everyone on the rock can read, that the café owners and the coastguard and the children read alike, so that nobody needs to be told, in the hour before a landing, that something has crossed the line of the sensors; and the cars begin to move toward the pier before the siren.

This is the island that the maps give as a dot off the shelf of Africa.

It is a frontier made of water and limestone, and because water keeps no mark and limestone keeps every one, the sea closes behind each hull and the stone below the lighthouse holds the scratch of a keel from twenty years ago, where the paint is still blue; and the apparatus writes its own kind of rock over both, in cable and concrete and light, which thickens a little with each season. Nothing here is hidden; everything is simply very difficult to see.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a trough of open water, which the charts shade a deeper blue than the shoals on either hand, and because the seabed climbs abruptly toward the south, the swell steepens over the rise and breaks white above a ledge no eye can find, and the island itself lifts out of that disturbance, a long limestone deck whose fields slope only one way, seeming to tilt its whole back to the north, so that the cliffs stand against Africa and the harbor opens toward Europe, as if the rock had decided, at some hour before any treaty was drawn, to face the continent that governs it, and to keep the other at its shoulder.

Lampedusa, which is nearer to Tunisia than to the province that administers it, which carries no river and almost no soil, which has learned to hoard rain in cisterns cut beneath the courtyards, lies low in the glare; from the sea it is a pale wafer, from the air a hyphen between two coasts, from the registers in Rome a point of entry with a number.

The town gathers along the single bay on the sheltered flank, and the fishing quay holds the middle of it, while the breakwater arm closes the water into a basin of oily calm.

Behind the quay climbs a street of flat-roofed houses whose shutters stay drawn until evening, and above them stands the radar mast, whose white dome turns without any sound reaching the lanes below.

Beyond the last houses the ground hardens into garigue, which the wind has shorn to ankle height and the sun has bleached to the color of ash, and nothing grows tall enough to cast shade when the light stands overhead; the only verticals are the aerials, which the salt has taught to rust in streaks.

The airfield, which was built to let military transports land on a rock too small for them, which still divides the island crosswise, takes the whole waist of the place, and the perimeter fence that follows it runs through what were once goat tracks, and beyond the fence the land falls again to the cliffs, and the cliffs drop clean to the water, deep enough for a hull to come in close before it strikes, though the swell that seems gentle from above gathers weight in the inlets and returns as a white shock.

From the headland one can see the cutters at their moorings, and the grey of their hulls repeats the grey of the quarried stone exactly.

The patrol craft put out at dusk to cross the first band of water; they go without lights; they are tracked from the mast, and they are tracked from satellites, and their courses are entered into a ledger that no one on the island reads, before the paper is filed in another country.

The coast guard keeps the eastern berths; the harbor police keep the inner mole, and where the two authorities meet the paperwork multiplies, so that a hull brought in at three in the morning is counted twice, and is photographed once, and is emptied by lamplight.

Farther inland, past the airfield and the water tanks, the reception center occupies a hollow in the limestone; the road to it bends out of sight behind a ridge, and the buses that climb it are white and unmarked, which the inhabitants recognize anyway, and which they watch without comment from their doorways; the hollow was chosen for the same reason the cisterns were, because it is a shape that holds what is poured into it, and because what it holds cannot be seen from the sea, nor counted from the water, however patiently a watcher waits offshore, while the light fails behind the island.

This is the geography of the place, which no map of the province has ever quite admitted.

The island sits at the hinge of two systems, which meet along no line that can be drawn in stone, and since the sea has no border of its own, the patrol routes are laid over it like latitudes, and the radar sweeps where the fences cannot go, pushing the frontier out to a distance that the eye from the cliff cannot measure, and the apparatus becomes a kind of weather over the water, which arrives and withdraws by schedules of its own; the rock, meanwhile, holds still and waits.

The channel that separates the two continents narrows here into a corridor of water barely a hundred kilometres wide, which the charts mark with a dotted boundary no current respects, and because the seabed rises toward the African shelf long before it reaches Europe, the swell steepens over the shallows and the horizon acquires a false solidity, so that the island appears from the south as a low grey wedge lifted on its own haze, an island that belongs geologically to Africa and politically to Sicily, and seems to exist in order to be arrived at, for everything built upon it has been built facing the water, and the jetties, which were cut for fishermen, have been widened and rewidened until the harbour can take a patrol cutter alongside a trawler without either having to move, though the cutter will move before morning, since the radar has found something low and slow eleven miles out, and the duty officer has already begun to dress.

The rock itself is limestone, porous and pale, scoured by a wind that arrives from the Sahara loaded with red dust, veined with cisterns older than any registry office, worn into coves too small to hold more than a single hull: and where the limestone falls away the water goes instantly from turquoise to a blue with no floor in it, where the depth sounder loses its patience, where the seabed is understood rather than seen.

Nothing on the island stands higher than the radar mast above the airfield; it turns without hurry, a white dish on a lattice tower, while beneath it the runway lies open to the glare like a bleached bone.

The settlement gathers around the Old Harbour in terraces of flat-roofed houses whose cisterns catch what little rain falls; behind them the scrub begins, a low grey vegetation that holds the thin soil together against the wind.

From the ridge above the cemetery one sees the whole arrangement at once, which measures perhaps twenty square kilometres and holds nine summer tourists for every winter resident, too compressed to permit anything to be hidden, since the coastline doubles back on itself at every headland; and the eye finds, at the southern edge, a compound that was never meant to be permanent.

The reception centre, which was built to hold four hundred people for seventy-two hours, sits in a bowl of ground called Imbriacola, and the road to it climbs past a fuel depot and a shuttered quarry, a road that the buses take at dusk, a road that the island's few hundred metres of asphalt cannot really accommodate, so the buses go slowly, and the dust they raise hangs behind them in the headlights, long enough for the next vehicle to drive through a wall of it before the air clears and the gate comes into view.

The agency that coordinates the surveillance keeps no permanent building here, preferring to lodge its officers above the port, and its aircraft are leased from contractors in three countries.

The equipment is designed to see rather than to intervene: the thermal camera on the breakwater sweeps a slow arc; the cutters carry transponders, and the transponders report to a screen in Warsaw; the helicopters refuel at the strip and lift again before the heat of the day makes the air too thin to climb through.

The sea between here and the Libyan coast is divided into zones of responsibility; the lines exist only in a treaty annexe, and when a hull founders inside one of them the question of who must go is settled by radio, by the fuel state of the nearest vessel, by the slow arithmetic of jurisdiction.

What arrives arrives mostly at night: the small boats come up from the south-southeast on the last of their fuel, and they are intercepted eight or ten miles out by a cutter that has been waiting on station, a cutter that rides without lights until the final approach. What is landed is counted on the quay: a procedure that has acquired, over two decades, the unexamined smoothness of any local trade that is performed daily, so that the blankets are stacked in advance of the stacking, the registration tent is raised before anyone needs it, and the ambulances park where they always park, facing the road.

Beyond the quay the ferry berth stands empty for most of the week, which is the only part of the port that keeps a published timetable.

At first light the whole island resolves into its two colours, the white of the stone and the blue of the water, and because nothing intervenes between them there is no middle distance at all, and the sea reaches the sky without any intervening line, except where a cutter drags its wake across the morning, and the eye follows that wake outward, which thins and loses itself somewhere south of the territorial limit: the wake closes; the water forgets it; the radar continues to turn.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows southward into a shallow trough, which the fishermen still call the corridor, and where the seafloor rises again after some ninety miles of darkness it throws up a last pale shelf of limestone, and on that shelf lies an island no bigger than a parish, set so far from the country that administers it that its hills belong, by every measure of rock and rainfall, to the other continent, whose dust arrives in April on a wind that scours the cisterns and leaves a rust-coloured film on the boats, until the whole place seems to tilt toward the south, as though the sea, having carried everything else there, had resolved to carry it too and were already beginning.

The island presents to the north a wall of cliff, which no vessel approaches willingly, which the charts mark in a dense hatching of soundings, which the pilots prefer to describe rather than to enter; the south is another matter, for there the land slopes in long dry terraces, there the coves open one after another in soft notches of white stone, there the water shoals so gradually that a hull may ground a hundred metres out and the people aboard must wade.

Above the largest of these coves the town climbs in low courses of flat-roofed houses, and the climb is not steep, so that from the harbour mole one can read the whole settlement at a glance like a ledger.

The harbour itself is a crooked basin, which a breakwater of tipped concrete blocks half encloses; inside it the trawlers lie three deep against the quay, where the grey patrol cutters take the outer berth by custom.

Beyond the last houses the ground opens into a plain of thorn and stubble, which the goats have cropped to the bone and which the sun bleaches by June to the colour of ash, enough to blind a man walking it at noon unless he keeps his eyes low; and across that plain runs the single asphalt road, which the buses use to reach the airstrip.

Set back from the road, behind a double fence of wire that the wind keeps singing, stands a compound of prefabricated blocks, which the official papers name a centre of first reception and assistance, and which everyone on the island simply calls the camp, for the word fits the thing, and no other word has managed to displace it, though the administration has tried for years to substitute a gentler one, since language here is maintained with the same diligence as the perimeter and both require continual repair.

Along the fence line a graded track keeps the inner ring clear, to allow the vehicles to pass at any hour, and floodlights stand at intervals of forty metres.

The apparatus does not end at the wire: it extends seaward, it has its own geography, it occupies the horizon as surely as the cliffs do and it is read, like them, from a distance by the colour of its hulls, which change with the authority they answer to, since the coastguard paints red where the finance police paint grey.

Out there the agency keeps its station: the aircraft turn their long ellipses above the convergence zone, and the radar on the headland sweeps a cone that reaches past the median line, that overlaps the Maltese arc to the east, that leaves, to the southwest, a wedge of water nobody claims.

Everything on the island is measured against that wedge: distances are given in hours of crossing, not in miles, and the inhabitants have learned a vocabulary of displacement that the mainland does not use, in which a boat is always either sighted or overdue; and the cemetery has grown accordingly, in a corner of the churchyard that the municipality enlarged twice, where the markers carry numbers instead of names, because the sea gives up a body long before it gives up the means to identify it, which would require papers to survive salt, and no paper does.

This, then, is the shape of the place, which a traveller grasps in a single afternoon and afterwards cannot forget.

A ferry comes three times a week from the Sicilian coast, which the islanders meet at the mole as a matter of ceremony, and when it docks the hold yields crates of bottled water and cement, and the gangway yields officials in pressed shirts, who come to inspect what has already been inspected; and when it sails again it carries away those who have been processed, whom the registers now describe as transferred, and the mole empties, and the lights on the headland come on one by one.

The sea between two continents narrows here into a shelf of pale water that the charts mark with a dotted line, and because the shelf lifts the swell and breaks it early, the island shows itself long before it is sighted, a low spine of limestone lying athwart the current, seeming to float rather than to stand, so that the fishermen who have worked these banks for generations and who still name the shoals in a dialect older than any treaty will tell you, if you ask them at the hour when the harbour lights come on, that the rock is not properly an island at all but a stranded piece of Africa that drifted north before the maps were drawn, and settled there, and stayed.

It is the southernmost parish of a continent whose capitals lie a thousand miles behind it, whose winters are rumours, whose summers press down upon the terraces with a weight one can almost measure; the airstrip runs nearly the length of the plateau, the cemetery leans against the wind, the boats that no longer float are stacked above the quarry like furniture in an emptied house.

From the cliffs at the western end the eye travels over nothing but water for a hundred and eighty degrees; there is no further shore to be read, only the grey seam where the haze begins and the horizon gives up its edge.

Below the cliffs the coves open one after another in a scallop of white stone that holds the light past sunset; the beach on the eastern flank, which the postcards favour, lies at the foot of a slope the colour of ash.

A patrol vessel stands off the headland each morning, grey-hulled and unhurried, and its wake writes a slow chalk line across the bay; it is stationed there to watch the southern approaches while the tramontana holds; its radar mast, whose lattice catches the first sun, turns without seeming to move at all.

Behind the port rises the long shed of the reception centre, its roof ribbed with corrugate too bright to look at near noon, its fences doubled in a manner the architects of such places everywhere have agreed upon, and higher still the aerials of the coastguard stand along the ridge, which the gulls have claimed, and which from the water resemble a thin plantation of iron, for the masts are slender and the guy-wires catch the glare, and the whole apparatus seems less built than grown, a crop put in to listen for engines before the engines can be heard, and to pass the bearing north.

The island is too small to absorb all this and too useful to be left alone, and so the machinery of the frontier has settled into the rock as naturally as the prickly pear.

Follow the coast road south out of the town: it begins as asphalt, then as gravel, and ends at a gate; a sign in three languages forbids photography, and a soldier raises a hand without rising from his chair, as though the gesture were weather rather than instruction.

The whole plateau is given over to this watching: the lighthouse marks the shipping lane, and the lane carries the freighters east while the smaller hulls come up from the south by night, by dead reckoning, by the loom of the island's own glow on the underside of the clouds.

What strikes the visitor first, after the dryness, is the ordinariness of the arrangement: the bar fills at seven, the ferry is late, the children play in the piazza beneath a mural whose paint has blistered, and nobody looks up; and then, climbing to the chapel, one sees the pattern entire — the harbour that holds the fishing fleet and the cutters together at the same quay, the slipway that takes both in winter, when the gales come round to the north-west and make it impossible to put out, and when the water in the channel turns the colour of slate.

There is a point on the ridge from which every one of these things can be seen at once.

From there the island resolves into a single object, a raft of stone that the sea has not yet taken, and because the light at that hour is level and the shadows run inland, and because the eye is lifted above the fences that divide the plateau into holdings, the fences themselves go out like threads drawn from a cloth, and the rock lies whole beneath the sky; only the engines carry up from the port, patient, intermittent, going on after dark.

The channel that separates two continents narrows here into a corridor of water scarcely eighty miles wide, which the old charts still mark with the soundings of sponge divers, and because the African shelf rises beneath it long before the European one begins, the seabed climbs toward the light and the swell shortens over the shallows, and so the island lies not with Sicily but with the coast opposite, a limestone raft that belongs geologically to the other side, seeming to have drifted north out of inattention, and the sea does the rest, which flattens and whitens in the lee of the cliffs until, every August, it turns the colour of smoked glass before the wind veers, so that the tourists photograph the bay until the light fails, and the ferries queue.

Lampedusa, which is three miles long and barely one across, whose highest ground would be unremarkable in any inland province, whose single town folds down a ravine toward a harbour too small to hold the traffic it receives, is a slab of rock laid flat on the current; the garrigue burns off by June, the goats have eaten what the wind left standing, and the roads end abruptly at the edge of a drop.

From the Albero Sole, the island's modest summit, the whole of it can be taken in at a glance: the northern coast falls away in a single unbroken wall, while the southern side crumbles into coves and landing places.

Along that southern rim lies the Spiaggia dei Conigli, which the guidebooks call the finest beach in Europe, and the loggerhead turtles return to it each summer, which is the one arrival nobody has thought to regulate.

Beyond the beach the land shelves into a plateau of thorn and dust, which the tramontana scours for eight months of the year and which no one has managed to farm, the soil being too thin to hold a root once the rain stops; and to the east stands the airstrip, which the island was given in order to be reachable.

The port, which the fishermen still use to unload lampuga and squid, which smells of diesel and brine in equal measure, opens between two arms of grey rock, and along the quay are moored the patrol craft of the Guardia di Finanza, which are painted a flat administrative green, which put out at dusk and return in the colourless hour before dawn, bringing in what they find, and logging it in a register kept at the capitanata, to be forwarded by evening to Rome, where the numbers are collated before anyone has thought to count them twice, and the file closes.

Behind the town, in the contrada of Imbriacola, a low compound of prefabricated blocks was built to hold four hundred, and the fence around it is three metres high.

The hotspot, as the European documents prefer to call it, sits in a hollow; the road to it is unsignposted; the gate is manned by the carabinieri and watched by the agents of Frontex, whose mandate is written in a language no one on the island speaks, though everyone understands it.

Twice a week the aircraft come down onto the strip: the deportees go out on the morning flight, and the island resumes its ordinary business, while the shops reopen, the nets are mended, and the bar by the church fills with men who have seen all of it before.

What the apparatus has made of the place is a kind of geography of its own: the coastguard station reads as a headland, and the receiving centre reads as a quarry, which the maps decline to shade in and which the satellite images show plainly enough; the whole island has been rezoned by attention, the radar mast on the ridge standing where a lighthouse would stand, which sweeps the channel every eleven seconds, which registers everything afloat within forty miles, so that nothing crosses unobserved, to be met and counted at the waterline, long before the hull touches the stones.

Southward the horizon holds nothing that the eye can fix, though the shore of Africa lies closer than the Sicilian one.

The water between is the most heavily surveyed in the Mediterranean, which the agencies describe in terms of sectors and zones, and because the vessels that cross it are unregistered, they appear on no manifest, and the screens record them only as contacts, which are resolved or not resolved before the morning; and the island receives them as it receives the weather, which arrives from the south and is not asked to explain itself: the cemetery on the hill has a section for the unnamed.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a trough of pale water, which the charts mark with a dotted line no keel has ever felt, and where the current runs northeast in summer the surface flattens to an oiled sheet and the horizon loses its seam, so that a low island rises out of it almost without warning, a flake of limestone tilted on its side, seeming to float rather than to stand, until the eye finds the cliffs that hold it down, and the cliffs in their turn break into coves on the southern flank, which open wide enough to admit a boat, if a boat survives the last thirty miles, before the wind swings and the swell begins to climb, to heap itself against the shoals, and the shoals answer with white.

Lampedusa is the name of that flake, a plateau of rock that the sea has gnawed from beneath, a slab whose soil is three inches deep in the best of its fields, a place that has never had a river to give it a reason to exist; yet the harbour on its sheltered side is deep and old, and boats have put in there since the Phoenicians counted their water in jars, since the Romans salted fish on the beach, since the Bourbons sent their first unwilling colonists across.

Seen from the air the island resembles a wedge driven between two weathers, and the resemblance holds in every season, since the north coast takes the gales on a wall two hundred feet high while the south lies open and low.

The plateau carries a single ridge, which runs the length of it like the spine of a sleeping thing, and the roads follow the ridge, which is the only ground that does not fall away.

Along the ridge stand the installations, masts and dishes and a radar dome that turns and turns, set there to watch the water before the water declares itself; and below them lie the hangars, which were built to shelter aircraft that no longer come.

The airstrip, which was laid down to serve a garrison, which has outlived three names for the thing it guards, divides the town from the interior, and beyond its fence the scrub resumes, a grey matting of caper and sea-squill and thorn that no goat has improved, a cover that hides the cisterns and shelters the last of the lizards, which turn the colour of the rock to survive the heat, until the sun lifts past nine and nothing moves on the stone.

Vehicles leave the strip at intervals to cross the island, and their dust hangs over the wall-lines for a quarter of an hour.

They go down to the quay to meet what the patrol boats bring, white hulls, grey hulls, hulls with a tricolour on the bow and a number beneath it, and the engines idle in the basin while the ropes go over.

On the quay the apparatus arranges itself by rank and function: the Guardia Costiera takes the near bollard, and the Finanza stands at the gangway, where a doctor in a paper gown waits with a thermometer, a nurse counts heads aloud, and a man with a clipboard writes nothing until the counting ends.

From the quay the road climbs past the warehouses to a compound of long low sheds behind a double fence: the gate is manned at all hours, the floodlights burn through the small hours, and the generator can be heard from the cemetery, which stands downwind on a terrace of red earth where the graves face the sea. The compound has an official designation, a hotspot, a word borrowed whole from another language, which nobody on the island translates, because translation would require somebody to decide what it is for, to say plainly whether it is a harbour or a hinge, now that the registering is done there and the leaving is done elsewhere.

All this the island carries on a surface you could walk across in a morning, if the heat allowed it.

The water that surrounds it is the clearest in Italy, a tourist blue that the brochures photograph in August, and when the season ends the ferries thin to two a week and the hotels shutter their terraces, while the boats keep coming out of the south through October, out of a dark that the radar reads as nothing; and the island goes on being two places at once, one of which is printed on postcards. The other has no postcards, and needs none.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows between two invisible walls of jurisdiction, and where the seafloor lifts into a shallow limestone shoulder it gathers itself into a single long island, with a scatter of rocks and sandbars trailing off its flank, and the island, which lies nearer to Tunisia than to any Italian province, seems to have been set down there in order to measure the distance that the water keeps between continents, a distance which is never fixed but swells and slackens with the wind, so that the crossing may take a night or a week, depending on whether the engine holds, and whether the swell decides to stay low enough to let the hull run.

The island itself is a slab of pale rock tilted toward the south, scoured bare of trees, worn down by salt until its ridges show the grain of old seabeds, and the few valleys that remain are too dry to carry a stream; its coast on the northern side rises in cliffs the color of bone, while on the southern side it opens into coves of white shingle, and there, where the land lowers itself almost to the level of the water, the boats have always come ashore.

Above the cove called the Rabbit Beach the ground climbs in terraces of broken stone, and the terraces end at a ridge of wind-flattened scrub, where the only shade is the shadow of a radar mast.

Along the spine of the island runs the single asphalt road, which carries everything from the airstrip to the harbor, and off it, at intervals, branch the white tracks that lead to compounds no map names.

The harbor lies in a drowned valley on the eastern flank, an inlet that bends twice and then widens, deep enough to hold the gray cutters of the coast guard, and it is from here that the patrols go out before first light, down a channel marked by buoys that the currents are forever trying to drag out of line.

What the traveler notices first, climbing from the quay, is the way the island's small scale forces everything into proximity: the fishing cooperative whose nets dry against the wall of the reception center, the customs office which shares its generator with the clinic, and above both of these the antennae, which stand on the highest ground where the goats once grazed, and which turn all night, and which carry the island's chief export, the data of the sea, to screens in Rome and in Warsaw, so that a hull of twelve meters is known as a contact long before it is known as a boat, and long before anyone aboard it can see the loom of the lighthouse.

The vocabulary of the place has learned to count arrivals, to sort them by vessel and by flag, and even the children repeat the hull numbers of the patrol launches.

Everything on the island has learned to be an instrument: the cliff to carry a sensor, the quay a gangway, the hangar at the airfield shelters a surveillance drone and the old military shed houses the registry, and the lighthouse on the western point still turns its beam outward, though the watching that matters now is done in silence and without light.

Nothing here is merely scenery; the stone is a vantage, the water a corridor, and because the island sits where two systems of law overlap, the authority that governs a given meter of sea may belong to Italy, or to a shared European office, or to no one at all until a rescue has begun.

Consider the geometry of it: the island is sixteen kilometers of rock, and around it lies a ring of contested water whose outer edge, drawn by lawyers rather than by tides, cannot be seen from any height on land; and consider further the boats that cross it, which set out from a coast three hundred kilometers to the south, which carry more people than any marine architect allowed for, so that the freeboard drops to the width of a hand, and the passengers must sit without moving for a day and a night, until a helicopter finds them at dawn and the long procedure of counting begins.

Whoever comes here for the summer water finds instead a landscape that reads itself aloud as a frontier.

The island receives them all the same, the swimmers and the saved, a limestone shelf that was never asked what it would be, and because the sea brings what the sea brings, and because the wind from the southeast raises a swell that no small hull was built to meet, the cemetery at the edge of town has a section of unmarked stones that the municipality tends, and the rest of Europe watches the island on a screen, a bright point off the edge of the continent, perpetually arriving.

The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here into a corridor of open water, a strait that the charts leave almost blank, and because the depth falls away suddenly past the shelf and the currents turn in long gyres against the coast of Tunisia, the sea arrives at the island already exhausted, carrying what it has gathered, so that the first thing a traveller notices, approaching from the north on the ferry that runs from Porto Empedocle, is a low pale ridge of limestone that lifts no higher than a warehouse roof and seems, as the hull swings east to take the harbour mouth, to have been laid down rather than raised, while the gulls, thickening above the breakwater until the air itself looks grained, go on calling.

Lampedusa, which belongs geologically to the African plate and politically to the province of Agrigento, which measures some twenty square kilometres from the cliffs of Cala Creta to the dunes of the Conigli, which has had no forest for a century and no river ever, seems to exist chiefly in order to be arrived at; and the arrivals accumulate in its registers whether the wind blows from the southeast across Libya, whether the sea flattens into the oily calm that the fishermen distrust, or whether the search-and-rescue vessels put out at three in the morning.

The island presents, to anyone who climbs the track above the airstrip, a surface scoured down to its bones: the scrub lies flat, the stone shows white, the few carob trees lean permanently northward because the sirocco has been pressing them that way since before the first lighthouse.

The harbour on the southern shore, which the land folds around in a hook of rock, holds the whole working life of the place: a quay, a fuel pontoon, the grey patrol craft that the Guardia di Finanza keeps moored bow-out and ready.

Beyond the quay a road climbs past the cemetery toward the hotspot at Imbriacola, which the maps do not name and the signage does not announce, appearing instead as a gap in the fence line, to be understood only when the buses pass; and behind it stands the compound itself, whose white containers are too regular to be mistaken for anything else.

The apparatus that administers the strait, which can be read off the landscape as easily as a watershed can, which has its own contour lines and its own drainage, is dispersed across the island and the water beyond it: there are the Frontex aircraft that circle at eleven thousand feet, there are the cutters out of Valletta and Catania that answer to no single flag, the radar mast turns above Albero Sole, and the tracking of hulls proceeds continuously, in order to establish where a boat was when it first became visible, since jurisdiction follows the sighting and the sighting is itself a thing that must be recorded.

All of this is arranged to make the sea legible, and the sea declines.

The barracks at the airfield are set low to resist the wind, the generators run, the floodlights come on at dusk and stay on until the sky pales, and the whole installation hums faintly through the night because the pumps that supply the fresh water never stop.

Nothing about the arrangement is concealed; it is simply unremarkable, the mesh has weathered to the colour of the rock, and the island absorbs it the way it absorbs everything, so that the cisterns, the chapels, the Second World War bunkers, and the turquoise bay the brochures photograph all sit in the same dust.

Past the last houses the land simply ends: the cliffs drop ninety metres to the water, the swell works at a line of caves whose roofs collapse every few decades and leave arches standing in the shallows. Out there the horizon is uninterrupted, a line that nothing crosses visibly, that the eye keeps returning to anyway, because to look south from Lampedusa is to look toward a coast one hundred and thirteen kilometres away, invisible in all weathers, though on certain winter evenings a smudge of haze lies along the bearing where it ought to be.

Here, then, is an island that is mostly edge, and a strait that is mostly waiting.

The wind drops at the turn of the year, which the crossings have always counted on, and when the glass rises and the fetch shortens, the departures begin again from Zuwara and Sfax, from beaches whose names appear in no itinerary, and the island prepares in its unhurried way, lifting out the blue hull that was broken against the mole last spring; the stone keeps its heat, the lighthouse turns, the registers open.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a trough of pale water, which the charts mark with a dotted line no current obeys, and where the seabed climbs again toward the south it throws up a long spine of limestone and lifts, at the spine's western end, a single low island; and Lampedusa, which belongs geologically to a continent it has never touched politically, seems to float rather than to rest, so that a traveller arriving by air, watching the runway rush up out of a sea that bears no mark of distance and offers nothing to measure against, must wait until the wheels strike before he can believe that the island has any thickness at all, and even then the belief arrives late.

The coast on the northern side is a wall of unbroken cliff, which the swell has undercut into galleries and blowholes, which no boat approaches in winter, which the fishermen name by the sounds they make rather than attempt to describe; the southern side slopes, so that the land tilts there like a held tray, so that every harbour, every slipway, every shelving cove faces the direction from which the crossings come, as if the geology itself had been surveyed by a ministry.

Between the two shores lies a plateau of dry fields and old terrace walls, stone laid on stone without mortar; and the wind, since nothing taller than a caper bush interrupts it, moves across this plateau with the flat insistence of water over a weir.

Along the eastern rim stands the aerial farm, whose white radomes sit on the ridge like eggs in a clutch; below them runs the perimeter fence, which follows the contour lines more faithfully than any footpath on the island.

The radar of the naval command sweeps a cone of sea whose radius exceeds the island's own length by a factor no one on shore finds comforting, and it continues to turn through the night in order that the watch officers, however empty the screen, may log the emptiness; which is itself a kind of topography, a relief map drawn to record what has failed to arrive.

The agency that coordinates the surveillance, which the member states fund in order to keep the question offshore, which has an office here no larger than a customs shed, maintains a pair of aircraft at the strip; and the aircraft, which lift at first light with their sensor pods already cooled, which fly the standard racetrack over the shipping lane and return before the heat builds and transmit their positions to a hall in Warsaw, descend again over the salt pans to land, while the island below them goes about the ordinary business of a Tuesday and the bakery opens at six.

The Guardia di Finanza keeps its cutters at the inner quay, grey hulls riding high, and the mooring lines slacken and tighten with the harbour's small breathing.

At the hot-spot above the town, built to hold three hundred, the gate stands open on a dirt yard; the fence carries no wire at its top and the gate is seldom watched, and nobody leaves, because there is nowhere on the island to go.

The registration hall occupies a prefabricated shed at the compound's edge: the fingerprint scanners glow faintly on their trestles, and each arrival passes along the row of them while a translator reads the questions aloud, and a clerk enters the answers, and a photograph fixes the face against a blue screen.

The cemetery lies on the far slope, past the last of the terraces; the older graves carry names and dates in ceramic, and the newer ones carry numbers painted on wood, numbers that correspond to entries in a register kept at the town hall and to bags stored for a season in the refrigerated container by the port. Beyond the wall the ground drops again toward the water, a slope that holds nothing but thistle and broken tile, a slope that the islanders cross in October when the first storms make the strait impassable and the boats stop coming for a while, as they always stop, as the year turns.

The sea from there shows no line at all, only the haze where the light gives out.

The island, which measures eight miles along its longest axis, is small enough to walk in a morning, yet the morning is never only a walk, because the road passes the quay and the quay passes the compound, and because every rise in the ground opens a view of the same water in which the same distances dissolve; and so the walker arrives back at the harbour with the sense of having circled something, something that will not reduce to stone and salt and the price of fuel. Everything here is at once a geography and an administration.
